Running on a Hot Day

Sardor, a track and field athlete from Termez (body mass 60 kg), is training for a marathon in the summer. To monitor his condition while running, his coach held one-hour training sessions in different weather conditions and recorded the results in a table. (The data have been simplified for learning purposes.)

Conditions that were changed: air temperature (°C), air humidity (%), whether he drinks water during the run (yes/no).
Results that were measured: volume of sweat produced in one hour (liters), water lost as a percentage of body mass (%), body temperature at the end of the run (°C).

Limits that are dangerous to health:
• Dehydration — if the water lost is more than 2 % of body mass.
• Heatstroke — if body temperature is above 40 °C.

No. | Temperature, °C | Humidity, % | Drank water? | Sweat, L | Water loss, % | Body temperature, °C
1 | 20 | 60 | yes | 0.9 | 0.4 | 38.0
2 | 25 | 40 | no | 1.0 | 1.7 | 38.2
3 | 25 | 60 | yes | 1.2 | 0.6 | 38.5

s0006: Heatstroke — in the body temperature column
s0007: Dehydration — in the water loss column
s0008: Dehydration — in the sweat volume column
s0009: No danger — all results are normal
s0011: We find the row in the table that matches exactly these three conditions — it is row 4.
s0013: The water lost is above the 2 % limit, so there is a risk of dehydration.

s0016: Answer: B) Dehydration — in the water loss column

s0018: In row 4 the body temperature is 38.6 °C, which is below 40 °C — there is no heatstroke.

s0025: Drinking water removes both dangers (rows 10 and 12)

s0056: Row 1 has 0.9 L and row 13 has 2.4 L — sweat did not decrease, it increased.

s0059: Explaining the biological function of sweating (thermoregulation)
s0060: Recall what happens to sweat on the surface of the skin and where evaporation gets its heat from.
s0061: When running in hot weather, sweat volume increases. What is the biological reason for this?
s0062: As sweat evaporates, it takes heat from the skin and cools the body, keeping its temperature normal
s0063: Sweat removes excess water from the body, which makes running easier
s0064: In hot weather the heart beats more slowly, so water leaks out onto the skin
s0065: Sweat shields the skin from sunlight and prevents heat from entering the body
s0066: Sweat → evaporates on the skin surface
s0067: Sweating produces liquid on the surface of the skin, and this liquid evaporates.
s0069: The heat needed for evaporation is taken from the skin and the blood.
s0071: Because of this, the body does not overheat — this is thermoregulation.
s0072: Answer: A) evaporation cools the body
s0073: The higher the temperature, the more the body sweats and the more it cools itself.
s0074: Sweat is not for getting rid of “excess water”; on the contrary, heavy sweating leads to dehydration (look at water loss in the table).
s0075: The heart beats faster during running; sweating does not happen because the heartbeat slows down.
s0076: Sweat does not block sunlight; its benefit is cooling through evaporation.
s0077: In a biological “why?” question, find the function of the organ or process for the organism: sweating is a cooling mechanism.

s0088: In row 5 the body temperature is below 40 °C.

s0097: Making a reasoned prediction for a condition not in the table, based on neighboring data
s0098: 50 % humidity lies between 40 % and 60 %. Compare the results of those two rows, which have the same temperature and water-drinking condition.
s0099: The coach wants to let Sardor run without drinking water on a day when the air is 35 °C and the humidity is 50 %. There is no 50 % humidity in the table. Is this run safe?
s0100: Safe, because no experiment was done at 50 % humidity
s0101: Safe, because in row 6 the body temperature is below 40 °C
s0102: Dangerous: in rows 6 and 8 (40 % and 60 %) water loss is above 2 %, and 50 % lies between them
s0103: Dangerous, because in row 13 the body temperature is 41.3 °C
s0105: We take the two rows with the same temperature and water condition whose humidity values surround 50 %.
s0107: In both cases the dehydration limit is exceeded.
s0108: 50 % is in between → water loss is also ~3 %
s0109: For a value in between, the result is expected to lie between these two values too.
s0111: So at 50 % humidity there is also a risk of dehydration.
s0112: The fact that no experiment was done does not mean it is safe; a prediction can be made from the results under neighboring conditions.
s0113: Only heatstroke was checked; in row 6 the water loss is 3.0 % — there is a risk of dehydration.
s0114: Row 13 has a temperature of 40 °C, 60 % humidity, and water drinking — these are different conditions, so it is not evidence for this question.

Crane Migration

Every year many birds fly from the places where they nest to the places where they spend the winter, and back again — this is called migration. Every spring and autumn thousands of birds, including cranes, pass over Uzbekistan. Each year volunteer observers count the passing birds at set locations, for example around the Aydar-Arnasay lakes. Scientists also catch some of the birds, put a numbered ring on their leg, and release them. Together, the places where ringed birds are seen and the volunteers' counts help to work out the birds' migration routes.

Most small songbirds fly at night, not during the day, when they migrate. During the day they rest and feed.

The two schematic maps in the picture show the routes of one species of crane, drawn from more than ten years of observations: Map 1 — autumn routes flying south, Map 2 — spring routes returning north. The thicker the arrow, the larger the flock that flies along that route.
s0126: The thicker the line, the larger the flock of birds
s0127: Explaining animal behavior through natural selection (evolution)
s0128: In an evolutionary explanation, look for the answer to the question “which individuals, with which trait, survived more and left more offspring?”
s0129: Most small songbirds fly at night during migration. This behavior developed through evolution. Which explanation is the most scientific?
s0130: The birds learned that flying in the daytime is dangerous and taught this knowledge to their chicks
s0131: Birds that flew in the daytime were caught more often by birds of prey, so fewer of them survived and they left fewer offspring
s0132: There are many insects in the air at night, so the birds can feed well while they fly
s0133: Birds that flew at night called birds of other species to join them on the journey
s0134: Behavior is an inherited trait, passed down generations
s0135: In evolution, it is inherited traits that are selected, not learned ones.
s0137: Birds that flew in the daytime died more often.
s0139: That is why, after many generations, flying at night became widespread.
s0140: Answer: B) survival and leaving offspring
s0141: The natural selection explanation is option B.
s0142: Knowledge learned during a lifetime is not passed to the next generation through genes — this is not an evolutionary explanation.
s0143: According to the text, the birds feed during the day; also, this does not explain why the trait spread through the generations.
s0144: Calling other species does not increase this species' survival or number of offspring — it cannot be a reason for selection.
s0145: Key words in evolution questions: “survived”, “left more offspring”, “the trait was passed on to the next generation”.
s0146: Identifying limitations of a data collection method and their effect on the results

s0149: Ringed birds become heavier and fly slowly, so they are counted twice
s0150: The volunteers write the results in a different notebook each year, so the numbers become too high
s0151: Many birds fly at night, so some of them are not counted and the number comes out lower than the real one
s0152: Cranes are large birds, so there are no errors at all in counting them
s0154: The observers work only during the day.
s0155: Text: many birds fly at night
s0156: So birds that pass at night are not seen.
s0158: This error makes the count lower than the real number — both the factor and its effect are clear.
s0159: Answer: C) flying at night → undercounted
s0160: The limitation of the method and its effect on the result are shown correctly.
s0161: A small ring does not noticeably change a bird's speed, and flying slowly does not cause double counting.
s0162: Which notebook the results are written in does not change the number — this is not a factor affecting accuracy.
s0163: Even for flocks of large birds the count is an estimate; they can fly behind clouds or very high — it is wrong to say there are no errors.
s0164: To find a limitation of a study, ask yourself: “Which birds might the observers miss?”
s0165: Comparing information on two maps and choosing the conclusions the maps support
s0166: Check each claim separately: is there evidence for it on the maps? Claims about information that is not on the maps at all (changes in numbers, shifts over the years) are not supported.

s0185:
Meteoroids and Craters

Pieces of rock and iron moving through space are called meteoroids. When a meteoroid comes close to a planet or a moon, it is pulled toward it. If the planet has an atmosphere, the meteoroid heats up from friction with the air, burns, and leaves a bright trail in the sky — we call it a “shooting star”. Many meteoroids burn up completely in the atmosphere. Those that do not burn up in time hit the surface and make a hollow — a crater.

At the Maidanak Observatory in the Samarkand region, astronomers observe craters on the Moon's surface. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so its surface is full of craters. Venus's atmosphere, on the other hand, is about 90 times denser than Earth's.

The picture shows three craters on the Moon's surface — K, L, and M — seen from above.
s0186: Three craters on the Moon's surface (view from above)

s0196: Objects with mass attract each other
s0199: The Moon's mass pulls the meteoroid and speeds it up.
s0200: Answer: C) the Moon's mass pulls it

s0202: Spinning on its axis does not create a force that pushes objects.
s0203: According to the text, the Moon has almost no atmosphere; and heating does not increase speed.

s0205: In a “why does it speed up?” question, look for the force acting on the object; for celestial bodies this is usually the force of gravity.

s0243: L is entirely inside K → L came later

s0248: That is the order according to the overlap rule.

s0251: L lies inside K, so it cannot have formed before K.
s0252: A rule from geology: when marks overlap, the intact (undamaged) mark is the newest and the damaged one is older.

A Study of Mountain Slopes

In a ravine in the Zomin mountains, students noticed an interesting difference: the north-facing slope of the ravine was densely covered with juniper trees and shrubs, while plants on the south-facing slope were sparse.

The students decided to investigate the reason for this difference. For one month they measured three factors on each slope:
• Solar radiation — how much solar energy reaches the place;
• Soil moisture — the proportion of water in the soil;
• Precipitation — how much rain falls on the place.

On each slope, two identical measuring instruments for each factor were set up in different places.

The students calculated the mean of the instrument readings and recorded the measurement uncertainty using the “±” sign:

Slope | Solar radiation | Soil moisture | Precipitation
North | 4100 ± 350 MJ/m² | 31 ± 3 % | 520 ± 45 mm
South | 7600 ± 450 MJ/m² | 17 ± 2 % | 545 ± 50 mm

s0258: So that one instrument measures during the day and the other at night
s0259: To take into account differences in conditions within a slope, make the measurements more accurate, and check whether the difference between the slopes is real
s0260: To add the results of the two instruments and double the total solar energy reaching the slope
s0261: Because the instruments were cheap, so the extra ones could be used up too
s0262: Conditions vary even on one slope
s0263: One spot may be in the shade and another in the open.
s0265: Several measurements make the mean more reliable and allow the uncertainty to be estimated.
s0267: Only then can we trust the difference between the slopes.
s0268: Answer: B) accuracy and checking the difference
s0269: That is the scientific purpose of repeated measurement.
s0270: The text says the instruments all worked the same way for one month; nothing is said about splitting into day and night.
s0271: The results are not added; their mean is taken — the energy received does not depend on the number of instruments.

s0293: A Fish Farm on the Syr Darya
s0294:
A Sustainable Fish Farm

People's demand for fish keeps growing, and this puts heavy pressure on wild fish in rivers and lakes. That is why an experimental farm on the Syr Darya is testing a sustainable way of raising common carp.

A sustainable farm must solve two problems: (1) growing food for the fish on the farm itself and (2) keeping the water clean. Fish waste builds up in the water and harms the fish themselves. River water flows through the farm all the time; before the water goes back to the river, the waste and excess nutrients in it (substances that algae and plants need to grow) must be removed.

The farm has three ponds (see the diagram). Water flows from Pond 1 to Pond 2, then to Pond 3, and returns to the river.

The farm uses the following organisms:
• Carp — the fish being raised; its favorite food is daphnia.
• Microalgae — microscopic algae that grow with only light and nutrients (they are already in Pond 1).
• Daphnia (water fleas) — tiny crustaceans that feed on microalgae and reproduce very quickly.
• Mussels — shelled animals that pass water through their bodies and feed on the microalgae and tiny particles in it.
• Reeds — plants that absorb nutrients and waste from the water.

The Ladybug — Protector of Cotton Fields

The ladybug is a small beetle with black spots on its red or yellow wing cases. It is common in the orchards and fields of Uzbekistan.

Ladybugs and their larvae feed on aphids (tiny sap-sucking insects). Aphids suck the sap of cotton plants, vegetables, and fruit trees, causing great damage to crops. A single ladybug larva eats several hundred aphids during its development.

At biofactories (biolaboratories), ladybugs are bred and their larvae are released into the fields. This is a way of fighting pests without poisonous chemicals.

One female ladybug lays several hundred eggs during her life. The body of a ladybug larva is covered by a hard outer covering (exoskeleton), and the larva molts several times as it grows. The picture shows the life cycle of the ladybug.

Fireworks: First the Light, Then the Sound

When there are fireworks on the evening of Independence Day, people first see the flash in the sky and hear the sound of the explosion a little later. Students in a physics club investigated this delay.

They tried changing two factors:
• the size of the firework charge (small, medium, large);
• the distance between the place where the firework exploded and the observer (km).

In each experiment, the time between seeing the flash and hearing the sound was measured with a stopwatch. The air temperature was about 20 °C. The results are in the table:

s0602:
Cotton and “Fast Fashion”

Many people are worried about the effect on the environment of producing clothes and throwing away old ones. The habit of buying cheap clothes often and throwing them away quickly is called “fast fashion.”

Cotton fiber comes from the surface of the seeds inside the cotton boll. Compared with synthetic fibers, cotton fiber needs less processing and breaks down more quickly in nature.

However, growing cotton requires a lot of water, fertilizer, pesticides, and other chemicals. In Uzbekistan, taking large amounts of water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to irrigate cotton fields has been one of the main causes of the drying of the Aral Sea. To reduce these problems, sustainable methods of growing cotton are being developed.

For a crop to be recognized as “organic,” it must be grown without synthetic fertilizers and pesticides; genetically modified varieties are not considered organic either.

s0661:
A Wind Farm in the Desert

A district administration is considering building a wind farm in a desert area. The wind turns the turbine blades, the turbine generates electricity, and the electricity is sent through a cable to the main power grid. At present the district gets its electricity mainly from thermal power stations that burn coal and gas.

Some of the district's residents support the project, while others are worried that it will harm the local natural environment.

The wind farm will be built in one of the four zones in the picture. The farther a zone is from the power grid, the more expensive it is to lay the cable and build roads.
• Zone A — every spring and autumn, very large flocks of birds fly low over this area.
• Zone B — home to rare (endemic) plants that grow only in this area.
• Zones C and D — common animals such as gerbils and lizards live here; they can easily move to neighboring areas.

s0736:
Loss of Biodiversity

“Biodiversity” is the variety of plants, animals, and other organisms living in a particular area or on the whole Earth.

The nature of Uzbekistan is very diverse: deserts, mountains, rivers, and lakes are rich in their own special species. But because of the drying of the Aral Sea, overgrazing of pastures, and other causes, some species are declining. Species in danger of extinction are listed in the “Red Book”.
